#253102 72 2006-11-11T18:28:52Z DemonzLunchBreak
^I respect you, winjet.

Anyways, the problem with the rating system is that people are unsure whether or not to rate "on a curve" where the median score (2.5) is an average map, or if they should rate the same way grades are given in school, where A's are ridiculously easy to get.

In my opinion there are several classes of raters:
Snipers - the people who are jealous and rate 0 or .5 just because.

N00bs - the people who give eveything 4.5 or 5 because they haven't seen enough maps or because they want the other author to rate their maps higher

People who are afraid to rate low - if these people don't like a map, they most likely won't rate it. They have armies of n00bs that they rated high willing to rate them high.

Old-timers - the people who have been around forever, have seen great maps, and rate lower than others necessarily think is fair. These people tend to rate on a curve.

And winjet, your math was a little off. On a curve ratings are based on GPA, where the highest is four, and the lowest is zero, therefore the median is 2.00, or a "c."

Quote: iangb, November 30, 2006 06:14 pm
I've never had a creationist to bash argue with.

Me niether. Let's begin.

To start with, there is no evidence to support the genesis of the old testament (at least not to my knowledge; I'd be very interested to see some)

Also, there is a great deal of evidence to support the big bang theory.
  • The universe is expanding
We can see this very clearly through telescopes...
  • Cosmic background radiation
The expansion of the universe causes it to cool. It also stretches light waves, making them red and, the farther away you look, infrared. For the universe to expand this way, it must have have started in a dense, high temperature point.
  • Cosmic Nucleosynthesis, or helium abundance.
25% of the universe's mass is helium, and stars alone could not have produced that much helium in the length of time that even science tells us the universe has existed. this indicates that the universe was at a high density and temperature during its creation.

Quote: Obby, December 18, 2006 02:42 pm
I disagree. Say you are standing in a room. You are alone. You are facing one direction and you see nothing in front of you. You do everything you can to make sure there is nothing there. There is nothing there. You close your eyes, and turn around. When you open your eyes, a cookie is there. Simple reasoning says that the cookie must have come from somewhere and didn't just appear by itself. Now, in this analogy, the "you" is humans looking back into our history to see where the universe came from. The cookie is the universe. When we look back far enough, past the beginning of the universe, we see nothing. This is represented by you making sure nothing is in front of you. When we look a bit later, we see the universe. This is represented by the cookie. We know the universe must have come from somewhere. Simple reasoning tells us that the cookie (universe) came from somewhere. To say that the universe just happened from absolutely nothing is actually going against logic, which was the goal of science. (to use logic to find the answer)

I disagree. The conclusion that the universe must, logically have a creator is a fallacious one. The assumption comes from the flawed principal of causality, which can't possibly hold true. By that reasoning, some preceding event must have created the creator, and something must have created that, and so on and so forth. This, to me, seems a bit presumptuous.

How is it more logical to assume the existence of a supernatural being that has no cause, than to think that maybe, just maybe, the universe has no cause?

From now on, be devoted to fighting the problems in your life. You can have any of those things, if they are what you truly desire.

You know what my other advice would be? As much as I love having you around, and trust me, that's a lot, you might want to consider restricting your computer time, or even unplugging it for a while. #14084 1 2007-02-17T04:07:24Z DemonzLunchBreak
This is just one giant mountain of frustration from me, that's been building up over the last couple of weeks. There are two vague areas of fake people whom I hate. The first is people who aren't true to themselves; people who put on acts every day, every word that comes out of their mouths is to project an image of someone else. Someone they're not. The second kind of fake person, the kind of person I'm angrier with now, are fake nice people. People who act like they're your friend, or at least on friendly terms with you. People who say bad things about you behind your back. These people are generally manipulative, arrogant, and deceptive. Or at least they have been, in my experience.

For example, I was talking with an aquaintence, someone I thought I was on friendly terms with, today. She's a friend of one of my friends, and we got to talking. I don't really want to get in to the specifics, but we made friendly conversation for a while, we talked about current goings on at our school, it was all a very pleasant experience. We talked about something that had been bothering me lately, something I was feeling down about, to a certain extent. I realized midway through this part of the conversation that this is what she had come to me to talk about. I ended up explaining to her why I was upset, and how I was then currently feeling. She gave me a complement, one that took me off guard a bit, but one that I appreciated greatly. Overall, a pleasant experience. So I thought anyways.

One of my friends talked to her later that day, talking about me, in which she remarked simply: "I don't really like him." This statement in and of itself would make very little difference to my life, and I would probably have ignored it, were it not for the element of deception, and of manipulation. It felt like she was being nice to improve my thoughts of her, to make me think that she's a better person. Well, it fucking worked. For half a day. I thought she was just... actually nice. I felt, in a weird way, kinda backstabbed by her when I found out about all this shit.

Fake nice people are just a giant object of hate for me. I can't fucking stand them.

I just felt like venting my anger here, hope you guys don't mind.

#14704 1 2007-04-03T04:14:17Z DemonzLunchBreak
What you are about to hear is a collection of ideals. I do not think that these ideals will ever realistically happen within human society. I do think that small incremental steps in this direction are possible. These are based upon my personal values, and so I would think it natural that people disagree with this to a certain extent. I'm not trying to convert you, or whatever. I think this would be an improvement, overall.

Laws
My idea for a perfect society is based upon the golden rule, "do unto others as you would have them do unto you." Everyone follows this rule. There are, however, no laws aside from this. There is one time this rule can be broken. See "Lawbreakers." Society will recognize that in order to maintain general happiness and order, no one should steal, no one should murder, no one should rape, no one should commit arson, etc. People recognize that others appreciate respect, and that respect begets respect. Respect for the possessions of others is essential. Property exists, and although much is shared throughout this society, there are some things that should not be shared. People are seen as mature enough to handle these issues, and to sort them out on their own. Compromise is extremely important when settling ethical disputes. If people disagree, and begin to violate the golden rule, they will be treated as lawbreakers.

Economy
Money has little value aside from little pieces of metal. Instead of exchange of money for useful services or objects, useful services and objects are traded for each other. Every job in society contributes its specific desirable object or service to society, while receiving objects and services in proportional amounts to those they contribute. Therefore, the people who have worked the hardest will have the most material possessions and services at their disposal. It is seen as their duty in society to disperse these resources to people who aren't able to provide for themselves, but the materially rich person has some degree of discretion, i.e. they can choose from a list of acceptable people.

Lawbreakers
These are the people who think it's a good idea to steal, rape, murder, and burn. Etc. They are discourteous. They mess with other people's stuff, basically, and in a severe way in which they do not want to be treated. Society does not contribute anything to these people's lives. These people are basically cut off from society, until they start to contribute. If they don't start to contribute after a predetermined amount of time, they are met with resistance. This society would be set in some distant futuristic age, and so really, people don't need to perform law enforcement, or anything. Robots just take these people, and drop them off on a jail planet. A jail planet is an inhabitable planet with no technology, no infrastructure, etc. Basically, society just leaves them there, and monitors their technological level.

Government and stuff
Everyone rules and has absolute power over one person. Their own self. That's it. No dominion. This society is designed to produce absolute freedom, as long as the people in question don't mess with the rights of other people. People are free to do as they choose until those freedoms clash.

Pro stuff
This system allows freedom. Freedom and equality, plus it operates under the assumption that everyone is mature, rational, and loves each other.

Con stuff
For this to work, everyone has to be mature, rational, and love each other.

Did I forget to cover anything?

I think that this would be a step up, but probably not perfect. What the hell is perfect anyways? Meh. Discuss.

This does bring up interesting ethical issues. I think that attempting to create "perfect" humans is silly, we'd create more problems than we'd solve, and it's a mess ethically. However, if genetic diseases such as Huntington's chorea, or Tay-sachs disease were curable, I'd be all for curing them. Of course, these are obvious genetic diseases, which do no one any good. Also, things like near-sightedness and other such problems, if curable, should be cured, because they provide no advantage, at least that I know of. I also think sickle-cell Anemia should be cured if curable, but only in populations safe from malaria.

I don't think that cosmetic genetic changes should be made, because this can lead to racial tension, and nazi-type ideals very quickly. If it must be done, cosmetic eugenics should be based upon a combination of the two parents' genes. This way, diversity is ensured, and no racial cleansing ever comes into play.

No one should be allowed to know the genetic information of another person, much like no one should be allowed to know another person's medical records. It is personal, and such knowledge could lead to genetic discrimination.

The reason that I ask this is because omnipotence seems impossible on many levels when criticized logically. God is described in the Bible as omniscient and omnipotent. Well, for starters, this statement is redundant. To know something is a type of power, and a god with all powers would be able to have such a power. Obviously. But wait! It gets wackier!

If god is omniscient, then he obviously knows what he will do next. He is therefore unable to do anything else. There is something that he is then unable to do, and he is therefore not omniscient or not omnipotent. That would work, except that omnipotence implies omniscience. Omnipotence therefore does not exist.

Another side paradox:

Could god make an object that he can't move?
Could god make a taco so spicy that he can't eat it?
Could god overpower himself at his most powerful?

If god can make the object, then he can't move it, therefore he is not omnipotent. If god can't make the object, then there is something that he cannot do, and he is therefore not omnipotent. The same logic applies to the taco, or the overpowering.

What do you think? Does this logic imply that omnipotence is impossible?

This is to address the "Lord, Liar, Lunatic" argument, concerning Jesus Christ, of Nazareth. Or, rather, why I think it sucks. I just felt like posting about it, because this argument really annoys me.

The argument:

1. Jesus claimed he was the son of god
2. To claim such a thing, one must be insane, lying, or the true lord.
3. Someone who lies about something so fundamental to their existence must be a bad person.
4. Jesus was not a bad person
5. Jesus was not a liar.
6. Someone must be extremely mentally unstable to think themselves the son of god, when they are not.
7. Someone who gives sound advice is not mentally unstable.
8. Jesus gave sound advice.
9. Jesus was not insane.
10. Jesus was not insane or lying.

.: Jesus is the son of the Lord, and/or the Lord himself.

The problems:

1. Actually, this is open to much interpretation. He could've easily meant that we are all "god's children," and so he referred to god as "father." Also, the Bible is not reliable as evidence. The entire premise of this proof is based upon the assumption that the Bible is true. The Bible can't be true cover to cover, because it's full of contradictions. The Bible is not reliable because it has been mistranslated. The Bible is not reliable because there are historical errors. The Bible is not reliable because of regular violations of the laws of physics, with no empirical evidence to support these violations.

2. This is a false trichotomy. There are other options. He might have been misquoted, for example. Also, none of these situations are mutually exclusive. Gods can lie, or be insane. Liars can be insane. All three could be true.

3. This is not always true. 'Good' people can make mistakes. Besides that, good and bad are opinions, more or less.

4. Again, subjective.

5. *Bzzzzzzzt* Wrong. He could have been.

6. True to a degree, yet certain parts of the brain can be almost completely depleted while others remain fully functional.

7. See above.

8. Well, yeah. Most of it.

9. Not necessarily true.

10. This is just a repetition, for the sake of rhetoric and clarity, so I don't think I need to address it twice.

The conclusion is completely inconclusive. This entire argument is logically weak, and I'm tired of fundies *cough* *macaddict* *cough* trying to use it to prove Jesus Christ. Yeah.


Edit:

Quote: Macaddict in a PM
The reason why is easy: If you don't accept that Jesus died and rose for your sins, nothing can save you from Hell, my friend. I tell you this because I care about you (sorta, I mean, I don't really know ya'), but I'd rather see you in heaven then in hell, dude.

I have an argument against your opinion of Jesus, if I may...

Jesus cannot have been 'just a good person'. Why? He claimed to be the Son of God. Either He was, or He wasn't. If He wasn't, was he lying, or did He really think He was? We have three distinct choices: He was either Lord, Liar, or Lunatic.

If He was a Liar, then why did almost all of His disciples go to their deaths saying that He did rise again? Surely someone desperate to save their hide would have spilled the beans. Would you die for something you knew was a lie? I think not...

If He was a Lunatic, then how come all of his sayings are so wise and profound? The teachings of Jesus are something a person with a crippled mind could not produce. No disorder could produce such conviction that He was the Son of God without affecting His other mental faculties.

That leaves us with the only possibility, as far as I'm concerned. Jesus was the Son of God.

The truth doesn't change based upon who believes or disbelieves it.

Also, both the Romans and the Hebrews site Jesus as a person, but not as the son of god.

The Bible is unreliable as evidence. There is no empirical evidence to suggest that your savior was actually resurrected. There are what, four, third-party, canonized, exaggerated, and contradictory accounts of Jesus's resurrection?

Condensed list of ressurection contradictions:

Who saw the empty tomb?

Last words.

How long was Jesus in the tomb?

More:

Matthew 28:1 states two women (Mary Magdalene, and the other Mary) came to the tomb; Mark 16:1 states it was three women (Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James, and Salome); Luke 24:10 agrees it was three women but gives a different list of three than Mark (Mary Magdalene and Joanna and Mary the mother of James); John 20:1 states it was only Mary Magdalene.

Mark 16:2 states "the sun had risen" at the time of this visit, while John 20:1 states "it was still dark."

Matthew 28:2 says "an angel" "came and rolled away the stone and sat upon it"; Mark 16:5 says the women encountered "a young man sitting at the right" of the tomb (rather than upon the stone); Luke 24:4 says they saw "two men" who "suddenly stood near them in dazzling clothing"; in John 20:1, Mary Magdalene saw nothing other than a moved stone.

There is also a discrepancy as to whatever dialogue occurred between this angel(s) or man (men) and the women: Matthew 28:5-7 and Mark 16:6-7 generally agree the women were told that Jesus had risen, and instructed to advise the disciples that "He has risen from the dead; and behold, He is going ahead of you into Galilee, there you will see Him" (Matthew 28:7), and ; Luke 24:6-7 contains no instruction to advise the disciples about an appearance by Issa in Galilee.

To whom did Jesus appear first? Mary Magdalene and the other Mary as Matthew 28:9 claims? Mary Magdalene only as Mark 16:9 claims? Cephas (Peter) and then the other disciples, as 1 Corinthians 15:5 claims? Matthew 28:9 claims that Jesus appeared before the women even had reported to the disciples what the found (or didnt) at the tomb. Also in Mark 16:9 the appearance to Mary Magdalene was before Mary made any report to the disciples. However, John and Luke report no appearance before the women reported an empty tomb to the disciples.

Which disciples went to the tomb? Peter alone (Luke 24:12)? Peter and John (John 20:2-8)? Did the disciples believe the reports of the women (or woman) and proceed to Galilee, as Matthew 28:16 claims? Or did they disbelieve these reports as Mark 16:11 and Luke 24:11 claim?

In appearing to the disciples, to whom did Jesus first appear? All eleven together (Matthew 28:17-18)? Two of them on the road, then to all eleven together (Mark 16:12-14 and Luke 24:13-31)? To ten of the eleven (minus Thomas) together (John 20:19-24)? To Peter, then the others (1 Corinthians 15:5)? The story recounted in John 20:25-29 is all premised on an appearance of Jesus before the disciples at which Thomas was not present! Matthew 28:17-18, Mark 16:12-14 and Luke 24:13-31 all disagree with John about any such meeting taking place in the absence of Thomas!

In Acts and the Gospel of Luke, the disciples were commanded to stay in Jerusalem and, in fact, met Jesus there (see Acts 1:4 and Luke 24:33, 47, 49). In Matthew 28:10 and Mark 16:6-7, the disciples are commanded to go to Galilee, and in Matthew 28:16-18, we are told they see Jesus (peace be upon him) there, not in or near Jerusalem!

Mark says that after appearing before the eleven disciples together in Gallilee, Jesus ascended to Heaven (Mark 16: 14, 19). Luke says Jesus ascended to Heaven at Bethany after walking with the disciples some time (Luke 24:50-51). John says Jesus appeared to the disciples at three times and that some of these appearances were near the Sea of Gallilee (Lake Tiberias) (John 21:1, 14). According to Acts the disciples were at Mt. #317271 40 2007-05-01T02:46:04Z DemonzLunchBreak
No, I'd say a more accurate analogy would be something like this:

Four friends say that their cat has come back from the dead. They have no evidence whatsoever. But hey, it's four people, right? RIGHT?!?!? Four is more than the one guy who disagrees with them, so they therefore must win, right?

They are taken into rooms, and questioned separately. One says that 511 people were watching when the cat walked up into the sky. One says 11 people were watching. One says that the cat first came out of the ground and showed up to two of the boys, one said that it showed up to two different people, one says it showed up to his mom first.

All but one of their stories must be blatantly false. That means that, logically, their claims are reduced to only one of the third-party, exaggerated, canonized fables that existed originally. One fable is not enough to hold up to both of the neighbor boys, whose stories have more empirical evidence to substantiate their claims.

If four people's story has the same basis, that doesn't make the story true. The story could have been completely wrong, or completely fabricated. If they contradict each other at fundamental levels, how can we know which is true?

They have a motive to fabricate the story. If they fabricate the story, people will believe in the religion that the gospel writers think think is right or good. If they can't keep fundamental details straight, it discredits all of them, for two reasons. The first is that we know that only one can be true, but how do we know which? The second is that the most likely explanation is that they fabricated the story and kept a simple premise, but they couldn't keep their details straight (I'm not accusing them of this, but it would certainly offer a counter-example).

If we call .999... an infinite geometric series S, each time adding (.9/10(n-1)) where n is the number of terms, then we can calculate the sum with the formula (.9)/(1 - .1). This is the formula for infinite geometric series.

(.9)/(1-.1)

(.9)/(.9)

1

Quote: Dave, 2007-05-16T16:41:23Z
That's not how infinity works. Infinity doesn't go on forever. It's at forever. It's not that it doesn't stop and it's not that it never gets to where it's going. Infinity is not a process. That's very important to understand before you can process the actual value of anything which relies upon an infinite series.

If we have an infinite geometric series, it's already infinite. It doesn't need to get there, it's already there, and has been, as soon as we write "S sub-infinity" or the sum of S when the terms are infinite.

What you're describing is silly. The idea that we need to, for some reason, actually add all the digits of the decimal to the end - it's a silly idea. It's already infinite. You obviously can't get there by adding one thing at a time. You have to postulate it as infinite, otherwise you can't talk about it in terms of infinity.

The formula for infinite geometric series comes from the formula used to calculate the sums of finite geometric series, which is as follows.

S at n terms = (G1(1 - r^n))/(1 -r)

However, Lim(1-r^n) = 1, as n -> infinity.

So, the formula for an infinite series is

S at infinite terms = (G1)/(1-r)
Where G1 is the first term of the series and r is the constant ratio.

Olcadan, I really don't like that story.

Quote
Prof: If you are referring to the natural evolutionary process, yes, of course, I do.

Student: Have you ever observed evolution with your own eyes, sir?


(The Professor shakes his head with a smile, beginning to realize where the argument is going.)


Student: Since no one has ever observed the process of evolution at work and cannot even prove that this process is an on-going endeavor, are you not teaching your opinion, sir? Are you not a scientist but a preacher?
You don't have to observe something to infer that it happened. You have to observe something to test it, so true macro-evolution isn't fact yet, however it's a decent theory. Anyways, the vast amounts of empirical evidence to support evolution don't make it absolute fact, but it's certainly not an opinion.

Quote
Student: Is there anyone in the class who has ever seen the Professor's brain?


(The class breaks out into laughter.)


Student: Is there anyone here who has ever heard the Professor's brain, felt it, touched or smelt it? No one appears to have done so. So, according to the established rules of empirical, stable, demonstrable protocol, science says that you have no brain, sir.


With all due respect, sir, how do we then trust your lectures, sir?


(The room is silent . The professor stares at the student, his face unfathomable. )


Prof: I guess you'll have to take them on faith, son.
Both the student and professor are silly. Possession of a brain has no bearing upon the quality of ideas that a person gives, and the students do have empirical evidence that the ideas exist. It, therefore, would be an acceptable inference to assume that the professor has a brain. His ability to think makes sense if he has a brain. However, he may not. This is possible, but astronomically improbable. To call it a statement of faith that he has a brain is preposterous, because all observed and tested humans have had brains, and brains have been their source of knowledge and thought.

Quote
Student: That is it sir... The link between man & god is FAITH .

That is all that keeps things moving & alive....... ......... ..
The first line is true, the second is ridiculous. Faith doesn't move boulders or shake mountains, sliding tectonic plates do. Faith doesn't keep a person with cancer alive, chemotherapy does.

Quote: Tsukatu@page 1, 2007-02-07T23:20:48Z
There is a tremendous difference between a purpose and a good idea.
"Procreate enough to maintain the existence of the species" is not a purpose, but a good idea.
"To show compassion to all other life" is not a purpose, but a good idea.
In order for there to be a purpose, there has to be something that set life into motion in order to accomplish a particular goal. So imagine a lifeless universe: this universe must have some sort of problem that some lifeless albeit thinking entity needed to solve, and so put created life in order to solve this problem or fulfill a particular purpose. Any purpose given to life that reflects back onto itself ("to treat all other life with respect") is not a valid purpose, for the same reason that an automaton that was created so that it could repair itself has no valid purpose - why make the automaton in the first place?

So if you're going to reply, I ask that you consider a purpose, and not something that's merely a good idea.

.: Free will and an omniscient being are mutually exclusive.

#16278 1 2007-07-17T17:58:13Z DemonzLunchBreak
It is often said that determinism and free will are incompatible. Here, in this topic, I will attempt to convince you otherwise.

Definition of terms:
Free will - the ability of a rational, sentient being to have complete influence over its own actions

Determinism - the belief that the universe follows one causal chain, and therefore the conclusion that there is one and only one possible future.

Incompatibilism - the belief that free will and determinism are incompatible. There are several kinds of Incompatibilists.

Libertarian - an Incompatibilist who believes that determinism is false.
Agnostic - an Incompatibilist who is not sure whether determinism is true or false.
Hard Deteriminist - an Incompatibilist who believes that determinism is true.

Compatibilism - the belief that free will and determinism are compatible. Compatibilists who believe that determinism is true are often referred to as "soft determinists."
-----------------------------------------------------------------
Each and every one of us, every day, feels the effects of free will. Many call this an illusion, or a quale. It's not. Every time that one feels as though he is making a choice, that is an actual choice. Every time that you are given two options, and are able, hypothetically, to choose either one, you have made a choice - completely regardless of which one you will choose in the future.

A person has free will when they make a choice in which an outcome is not forced - either through coercive means or through actual physical violence. The laws of nature are not sentient. They cannot force you to do something. Because an action is not forced, the choice is therefore free, and the rational agent has free will.

Not only are determinism and free will compatible, but free will requires determinism. The reason I say this is that the incompatibilist definition of free will would require a spontaneous and unpredictable result to every decision. Causality would have to be broken at some point - meaning that it is not the person who made the decision. People make decisions based upon their desires and values. Their desires and values are caused by a thing X. If their desires and values are not caused by some X, then they are not properly that person's desires and values at all!
------------------------------------------------------------------
Note: this argument for compatibilism does not apply to theological determinism. This is because of the nature of theological determinism. Theological determinism depends on the idea that a rational, sentient being created everything and began the causal chain, and a rational, sentient being can force one to do something, and does apply force when beginning a deterministic causal chain.

Imagine such a robot:
The robot is designed to dig a hole in the ground. The robot receives sensory input and assesses the plot of land it has been told to dig up. The robot then considers the means by which it could accomplish this task - after some processing, it determines that the functional methods of digging up the dirt are with its hands and with a nearby shovel.
The robot is clearly presented with a choice.
The robot then considers both options and decides which method is most effective. After weighing both options, the robot has determined that the shovel is most effective, and chooses the shovel.
If you were to put the robot in the same circumstance multiple times, he would pick the shovel every time. Quote: Atilla, 2007-07-18T03:17:28Z
Eh? Being a quale does not mean something is an illusion. A quale is the perception of something. If someone else breaks a leg, you know that the leg is broken, and that it would hurt, but you don't experience the feeling of having a broken leg itself. That is, you do not have the quale of having a broken leg. The typical example is the redness of red. We can measure the wavelength and so on and assert that light is indeed red, but this won't let a blind person experience how seeing the colour red feels. A quale is the sensation a thing creates in a given observer, not the thing itself, or a property of the thing. Qualia are by definition subjective.

#16410 1 2007-07-26T18:47:24Z DemonzLunchBreak
An argument that I see so frequently used by theists is that atheism leads to moral relativism, and that theism does not.

There are some problems with this.

1. The Euthyphro dilemma.

"Is what is moral commanded by God because it is moral, or is it moral because it is commanded by God?"

The first part of the dilemma is that if morality is commanded by God because it is moral, then there is an external basis for morality, beyond God, and human kind should also be able to discern this, given enough time and knowledge.

The second part of the dilemma is that what is moral is moral because it is commanded by God, then "moral" and "good" are just arbitrary values and subject completely to God's whim.

2. Inherent moralities exist.

Even if God descended to Earth right now, and commanded upon us that slavery was morally good, most of us would instantly realize that this is not so. This could mean, as far as I can discern, one of two things.

a. There is some rational or intuitive external basis for morality, and humans have knowledge of it.

b. Morality is completely arbitrary and subject to emotional values, and we are all therefore emotionally similar, while God is emotionally different.

3. The indeterminate nature of divine mandates.

Divine mandates are not useful as the only source of morality, because they are intrinsically vague and indeterminate.

For example, the sixth commandment says "Thou shalt not kill," but this is far too vague to be the only source of morality concerning killing. Does it mean that you can't kill fetuses? Or is God referring only to people? or Plants? or all three? or None?

These types of laws cannot be the only basis for morality, because they leave gray areas and complete blanks.

On the subject of Altruism as an evolutionary trait:

People are far more likely, even in extreme acts of altruism, to sacrifice themselves for people that they are related to. This means that the two people share many of the same genes and that those genes are passed on to the next generation. Also of note is the fact that the most common extreme altruistic action is a parent sacrificing themselves for their own child, which also makes sense from an evolutionary standpoint, because the children are the genes' future.

Many a physicist will tell you that the law of universal gravitation could never be violated. Science (the sheer act of observation) tells us that, eventually, we need to be able to infer natural law from observations--otherwise those observations are useless. Science indicates that even though the periodicity of elements has not been proven out to the millionth proton, that we should accept these patterns as law. We don't need to directly observe element 120 (which does not yet exist). Available patterns indicate it bears atomic characteristics to beryllium.
Yes, a great deal of science rests on induction. Science also recognizes that everything it comes up with is tentative. "Doubt may be an unpleasant condition, but certainty is absurd," as the saying goes.

Scientists who tell you that universal gravitation could never be violated must not have read anything by Karl Popper. Those scientist are going about it the wrong way. The point of science is not to ascertain absolute truths from observed patterns - it's to develop the most accurate model possible, while recognizing that that model is anything but absolute.

We should not accept gravity as law. We should accept that something very, very similar to gravity is happening and has happened and is probably, by all means of reckoning, going to continue happening. Things fall. This is obvious. The interpretation that we've developed is the theory of gravity. It's a damn good theory, but it's not complete.

Yes, we think that element 120's gonna be a whole lot like beryllium. It makes sense to believe that it does - but it's important to recognize that that knowledge is tentative.

Science also uses deduction as frequently as it can, and eliminates inductive reasoning in any possible place (modus tollens).

#364855 7 2007-09-14T04:55:47Z DemonzLunchBreak
My advice?

Relax.

Yes, it is good to try hard to be a great mapper. What's bad, though, is when you worry too much about not living up to some standard that you set for yourself. Don't worry about becoming "great." If you stick with it, you'll find your own style - and that style may be "great."

"Greatness" is sort of a subjective quality, though. What one person considers "great" could be garbage from another person's point of view. Making a map that you are happy with is far more important than attempting to please as many people as possible and/or receive a high rating. A rating tells you almost nothing about a map. People rate differently, people snipe, people over-rate - the rating system is not a good way to determine how much fun a map is.

Don't care too much about not being "great." Don't care too much about ratings. What you should care about is how you feel about your own map, and how much fun that map is to play.

As I have also addressed, even an omnipotent being has limitations, if his definition is at all meaningful. Any definition, by, er, definition, limits that which is being defined. A definition is, essentially, a set of limitations which distinguish a thing from all other things. For example, if I define God as "omnipotent, omniscient, and omnibenevolent," the very moment God fails to meet these requirements, he ceases to be God. This is therefore a limitation on the concept of God, because it is something that God cannot do.

If you define something as "without any limitation whatsoever," your definition is an inherent contradiction. This is because if that thing is truly without limit, then it cannot ever be limited, which means that it is unable to do something, which means that it is limited. You may as well define this thing as "a square circle" or "an invisible pink unicorn."

Edit: If that last paragraph was a little confusing, I'll put the thrust of it into syllogistic form.

1. If something is without limitations, then it cannot have limitations.
2. "Not being limited" is a limitation.
.: Something without limit both has limitations and does not have limitations.

Edit:

#392401 24 2007-12-22T19:35:59Z DemonzLunchBreak
Pascal's wager is garbage.

Beliefs (or the vast majority of them) are not choices. Most people will believe what they see, and believe what is proven to them. They cannot do otherwise. That's problem numero uno - it'd be completely impossible for me to adhere to Pascal's wager, even if the rest of it made sense.

The next problem I have with the wager is that it presumes that the only options are either that a Christian/Pseudo-Christian God exists or that no God exists at all. However, it ignores the possibility that a god may exist that rewards non-believers, or punishes believers. There might be a god with an ironic sense of humor, who creates an atheist heaven. Or, you know, Thor might smash you with Mjolnir. For every god that humans believe in, there are infinitely many possible gods that we haven't thought of yet, and for every god that someone believes in, there are scores that are willing to punish that person for his/her beliefs.

Also, Pascal's wager assumes that, if the Christian God exists, he will not notice that you believed in him only to be rewarded. I'm not sure he'd be cool with that.

Personally, I think the solution to these kinds of issues isn't to socialize every service that we're having trouble providing from the private sector - the solution is to provide better information to the consumer. To the best of my knowledge, there's no Vehix equivalent for the healthcare market, which allows the companies to practice whatever lousy service they want without creating an incentive for other companies to improve. If information is made available to the general populace, companies that do poorly will soon be in fierce competition with companies that provide better, more comprehensive service.

Without the competition of the free market, the healthcare field loses most of its incentive to improve the services it provides. I mean, you could argue that the state's program would be in competition with other charity services, and therefore have an incentive to improve, but then what's the point of giving all that money to the government, anyway? If the money can be distributed by private charity services, then there's no reason at all to have universal healthcare.

Quote: Obby, 2008-02-29T00:34:12Z
God's omnipotence allows Him to create square circles while not creating them at the same time. Anything humans can name, logical or not, God can do. Just because we don't understand something doesn't mean it can't be true.
And your beliefs are both true and untrue! The universe is a creampie, while simultaneously a sticky lawn chair.

All of these propositions are true, because God made it that way.
(Or, in other words, you have to toss every law of logic out the window the minute you accept a contradiction as possible).
------
One could argue that God created the laws of the universe, and therefore isn't bound by them - but even that is not a sound argument. First of all, that is an attempt to make a deductive argument, and therefore already assumes that rules exist (the rules of logic). This is the kind of borrowed-concept argument that Obby and Exuberance are making. One cannot proclaim that God is beyond human capability to reason without attempting to utilize the concept of reason (and, as far as I know, both Obby and Exuberance are human). Therefore, they invoke the very means of pursuing the truth that they try to explain away.

Also, if God created the laws of the universe, he would have to do so by some means. There has to be a way for him to create it if it came into existence by his hand. If that means is random, then God did not truly create the universe, random chance did. If that means is not random, then there must be some kind of rules governing it (e.g. the rule that the universe doesn't come into existence randomly). Since the rules exist, either God created the rules, or he didn't. If God created the rules, then the argument reaches an infinite-regression of rule creating, which is problematic. If God didn't create the rules, then I think that shows that there are things he cannot do.

Basically, I think the only good definition for omnipotence would be "the ability to do anything logically viable." I think God could be omnipotent, but I don't think he could create square circles.

I don't accept induction as valid for rational reasons. I do it for pragmatic reasons. I can't survive if I don't accept (or trust, or whatever) that water will make me stop being thirsty. I can only have that belief if I use inductive reasoning. I want to survive, so I choose to trust induction when necessary.

I guess you could almost treat it as an axiom. I can't prove that induction proves things, but if I assume that the universe follows some kind of pattern, then inductive reasoning can approach truth, kinda like 1/x approaches zero as x approaches infinity. Depending on the degree of accuracy I need with my truths, I can use more information or less. You can't get absolute certainty about things in the external world (empirical stuff), but I'm willing to settle for less if it means I can eat food and sleep at night and at least have a guess about how the world works.

Karl Popper tried to solve the problem of induction. You might want to have a look at his work, Ian. Then again, I don't think what he proposes is really a solution. It's more of a way of avoiding the problem.

The only medication that works against it anymore is a powerful antibiotic that makes the pneumonia go away, but brings my grandma close to dying.

The pneumonia comes and goes. Every few months, she'll get it again. There's not very much to be done about it. Even the nuclear antibiotic only makes the sickness go away for a while. I found out a couple hours ago that she got sick again, except that this time, my family and the doctors have elected not to treat her. This means that her death is guaranteed, as far as I can tell.

I've been struggling with thinking about this stuff. My first reaction was denial. Not outright denial - I knew that what my parents were saying was true. It was denial of thought about it. I went into emotional lock down. I couldn't really think about anything that was happening.

There really was no chance that she would get better after that kind of brain damage and that length of time. I hate that it had to come to this, but I support the decision of my family to let her go.

#444633 12 2008-06-15T01:19:44Z DemonzLunchBreak
Hmm, let's see. About religion... I would say that it's generally a negative thing, because it supports intellectual dishonesty and general irrationality. Mysticism (an idea that most religions advocate) holds that there are other ways to learn about the world, apart from reason and observation. This philosophy is anti-reality and destructive. Most religions give people bad advice, too. Morality doesn't spring forth from religion as many would claim. Normative ethics can be determined through purely logical means. Although it may not have been their original intent, many religions have been modified in order to control people, take money from them, or both. I believe that these things are true because I have observed the world, and I've read the holy books, and this is what I got from them.

About god... "god" is defined a number of ways, and I have different thoughts about different god-type beings. I believe that many gods have been deliberately defined in ways that are not verifiable so that religious people can go on believing in them. The idea that "God works in mysterious ways" would be an example of this. If it's so mysterious, there's no way to know that it's god who's doing the work in the first place, and if something bad happens, we can just say that it's God's mystery, instead of actually thinking about the implications. So, yeah, most gods are generally unverifiable, which makes the whole idea essentially useless.

Many concepts of "god" are inherently contradictory. Defining god as "outside of time" would be an example. God, as I understand the concept, is the creator of the universe. A being that... does stuff... has to exist within time. God cannot be conscious if he doesn't exist inside some dimension of time, because consciousness is a process, a process is a series of events, and that series could only take place in some kind of time. Another sentiment that I hear quite often is that god is immune to the laws of reason. Statements like this are completely ridiculous, and are necessarily false. A statement that follows the form "[blank - noun] is [different blank]" assumes that the laws of reason apply to whatever it is that you're talking about. The axioms involved are so basic that I know of pretty much no human that would deny them.

So I'm an agnostic atheist toward some gods, but I think it's impossible for some versions to exist at all, making me an anti-theist with regard to those gods.

I believe that invoking the supernatural in general is not a good way to explain things. In fact, I would say that supernatural explanations aren't really explanations at all. A supernatural explanation does nothing to explain how or why something happened. Now, let me be clear about this. If a ball drops and someone says "it dropped because there's a natural force that makes stuff drop" that's not really much more of an explanation than "it dropped because Jesus rays hit it down." Where these two paths differ is in testing and learning more about the dropping ball. If there's a natural law that makes things drop, then we can test it and develop mathematical models and the like. We can investigate further. Saying that unverifiable, untestable things, like "Jesus rays" hit stuff down doesn't provide a direction for exploration. We cannot examine or improve explanations which we cannot test. This is why the supernatural is a useless idea.

I have more thoughts, but I don't really feel like typing them. If you want to know what I think about something, feel free to ask.

#445014 29 2008-06-15T19:25:25Z DemonzLunchBreak
Oh, yeah. For irreducible complexity, I have an argument by analogy.

It's possible to build a stone arch with nothing sticking the stones together (example). If you remove any one of the stones, the whole arch collapses. The arch is therefore irreducibly complex. Removing one part makes the arch "die." However, it's possible to make a big pile of stones into an arch by removing the stones from the center, leaving only the loose arch on top. Similar arguments can be made for biological constructs. A nervous system might be irreducibly complex, but there might have been (at some point in evolutionary history) a "scaffold" of sorts that kept the nervous system functional while necessary parts were evolving. When the nervous system's new parts develop, they work so much more efficiently than the old "scaffold" parts that they completely replace the scaffold, and it is no longer necessary, and so it often goes away.

Showing that something is irreducibly complex doesn't give evidence for a designer. As I have just shown, evolution can produce things which are irreducibly complex. Also, many things that are called irreducibly complex really aren't. Probably the most notorious example, the eye, isn't irreducibly complex. You can remove the lens, for instance, and they eye still functions. It doesn't function as well, but some vision is preferable to no vision at all, and so it could have evolved that way.

Incluye: You don't have to stop, I'm just telling you that you should use evidence in a scientific discussion.

Quote: SkyPanda, 2008-06-16T13:37:21Z
My specific issues with 'big bang' theory concern only the areas where scientific knowledge is insufficient, such as the time before and during the existence of the singularity. It is the incompleteness of the big bang theory, i feel, that makes it implausible. I'm open to be convinced otherwise


There's a problem, here. Theories, by definition, only explain a specific range of data (we don't have a theory of everything). It makes no sense to reject a theory because it doesn't explain data that it wasn't developed to explain. Evolutionary theory, for example, does *not* explain the origin of life - abiogenesis does. But if you think the origin of life is suspect, that does not give you any good reason to doubt evolution's truth, because evolution doesn't deal with life's origin, only what happens once life exists. Similarly, the fact that there are unanswered questions in cosmology doesn't mean that you can reject the big bang. The big bang theory was developed to explain phenomena like the spiral shapes of galaxies, or the expansion of the universe, or cosmic microwave background radiation (well, that was predicted, but still...). The Big Bang explains all of these, as it was developed to do. It may not explain everything about the origin of the universe, but that doesn't lessen its truth. What happened "before" the singularity (if there was a singularity - see below) may not really be defined, anyway.

Second, not every Big Bang model starts with a singularity. Some models start with an approximate singularity, just a hot, dense center.

Well that's obvious. Of course it's an adaptation. Adaptations are the stuff that evolution is made of. Evolutionary pressure causes organisms to change or go extinct. When the bacteria were put into an environment with nothing to eat but nylon byproducts, they either had to develop a way to eat the nylon or die. That's exactly how evolution works. It's not always life or death scenarios, but maybe a species isn't doing as well as it could be doing, and therefore has evolutionary pressure to catch up with its competition.

Quote: incluye, 2008-06-17T22:44:39Z
Well, precisely my point. If the nylonase lost its ability to metabolize nylon byproducts after being removed from an environment containing them, I would see that as its ability being an adaptation as opposed to an example of evolution.
That's a false distinction. Adaptation is a word you'll hear a lot, if, you know, you take a biology class or something. Adaptation is a word used by every evolutionary biologist since Darwin. But, see, nylon-eating bacteria are only one mutation different from the bacteria that they came from. Undoing one mutation is unlikely, but it will probably happen if you give it enough time and evolutionary pressure. But let's say the nylon-eating population mutates again... and again. The chance that these mutations will be undone as well as nylonase grow exponentially smaller. Eventually, after enough mutations, the evolutionary pressure could change, but it would be essentially impossible for the bacteria to change back into what they once were because they would have too many mutations to undo.

This shows that you don't understand what evolution is.

Evolution is *not* pure chance. It would not work if it were random, and no reputable biologist would claim that evolution is random. The entire point is that there is non-random selection in nature. If creatures lived and died randomly, they could never improve or adapt to their surroundings, because the organisms that are less fit would have an equal chance of surviving and producing offspring. Evolution, instead of claiming that selection is based on pure chance, claims that organisms live and die because they were fit enough to survive or they were not fit enough to survive.

Now, there is a random element to evolution. Mutations are (kind of) random. But mutations aren't all there is to it. Mutations are just a way for organisms to change. Without natural selection, mutations would be useless.

No, nylonase is a group of enzymes. Nylon-eating bacteria use nylonase to digest nylon by-products. This isn't a particularly important distinction, though.

Quote: incluye, 2008-06-18T17:28:28Z
But it's still a bacterium. Are mutations ever - and I mean ever, in absolutely any circumstances - going to significantly advance it to a higher life form? Is the bacteria ever going to evolve into, say, a plankton, through countless mutations? (Many mutations are harmful or even deadly to the organism.)
Given enough time, it's certainly possible. However, there's not very much pressure for it to become more sophisticated. It's like asking if humans will ever evolve wings - it's theoretically possible, but it would take a huge amount of time, and right now there's no mechanism in nature that favors humans that produce slightly more lift. Most of the niches for flying creatures are taken up by birds, and they're much better at it.

Nylon-eating bacteria have no pressure to change into plankton. Or, really, to even take a step in that direction. Plankton have been doing what plankton do for millions of years, and have gotten good at it. For there to be pressure on a nylon-eating bacteria to become a plankton, the niche that plankton occupy would have to open up. For instance, there could be some disease that kills all the plankton in the world (probably not going to happen, but humor me). In that case, a step in the right direction would be extremely favorable to an organism, because there's nothing competing for the food that the plankton used to eat, and plankton's predators have nearly gone extinct, etc, etc, etc.

Quote: incluye, 2008-06-18T17:28:28Z
Yeah, maybe there was some kind of "scaffold" for amino acids to assemble themselves. But as far as we know, it hasn't been discovered yet. I think that's a fairly important discovery to have, because without it, evolutionists cannot explain the emergence of DNA.
Right. That stuff is tentative. The origin of DNA was so long ago that the best that anyone can do is make guesses. That doesn't mean that you can say "science has not found X, therefore evolution is impossible." That's called argument from ignorance. You also cannot conclude, since DNA's ancestors haven't been found, that a designer put DNA there.

That being said, there are many good guesses that don't involve a designer. It's not really possible to prove that they're true, but one can make an effective argument that they're possible, which means that the lack of one concrete answer to this question cannot be used as an argument for a designer.

#447222 66 2008-06-21T23:13:07Z DemonzLunchBreak
Southpaw is equivocating, I think.

A table is objective. It exists as an object. That's what "objective" means. Human opinion about a table doesn't change how it exists or the properties that it has. That being said, those things are not knowable without evidence that also comes from objects. However (and this is the mistake that Southpaw's making), an inability to know the specific attributes of the table does not make the table "subjective." The table exists as an object. It has specific properties that our thoughts cannot change. It is not a concept or thought.

A lack of evidence doesn't make something subjective. The claim "God is Omnipotent" is not true or false because someone thinks that it is true or false. A person's *beliefs* about god are subjective, but whether or not those beliefs reflect truth does not change depending on what people think. It's misleading if you pretend that a person's beliefs about something are the same as the thing itself. Beliefs are subjective, whether or not they're true (when they make objective claims) is not.

I'm not really worried about this. I run XP and ubuntu on my current computer, and I'm probably not going to get a new laptop any time in the near future, so this change probably won't affect me. When I get a new computer, odds are I'm going to get a PC laptop and dual-boot a linux distribution and Vista. I prefer ubuntu to Windows, but I keep windows around because there are some programs that I want to run that don't do so well with an emulator - mostly games - although with WINE and DOSbox I can convert about 50% of my games to linux.

I don't want to get a mac because I am not willing to spend the money/do not have it. That... and I can do pretty much whatever a mac user can do using free, open source programs. It's rumored that linux is hard to use if you're not a hardcore computer user, but with ubuntu this is simply false. I haven't needed to do anything highly technical to get what I want out of my OS.

The reason these arguments over operating systems are dumb is that the average computer user does pretty much the same thing no matter what operating system they use. Most people want internet, word-processing, spreadsheets, slideshows, and maybe a few games. For people who do other stuff, stuff that's beyond what the average computer user does, it actually makes sense to have a preference, but it's dumb to say that any one operating system crushes another in all categories. My friend's dad makes icons for microsoft, but he uses a mac. From what I've heard, pro image-makers tend to use mac software. My dad, on the other hand, writes software. You know, software that he can actually sell (runs native in windows, if you haven't figured that out yet). And for him it's certainly advantageous to use windows as his OS of choice. I use linux (mostly) because it's free and I only sort of have a job so I can't really pay for software. I also like to know what I'm putting on my computer, and I like to be able to adjust it to fit my purposes. Ubuntu lets me do all of this, so it's the best OS for me. If you want a server or supercomputer, it's sure as hell better to run linux than anything else.

Also, I'm thinking about changing distributions. I want something that takes up little disk space, is open source and customizable, and is designed primarily for speed on old, crappy toshiba laptops. GNOME desktop is preferable, but I'm open to KDE as well. Any linux fanboys out there that could help me?

Edit: I'm downloading puppy linux right now. I'll let you guys know if it turns out well.

Then I suppose it would be tiresome to argue against it - anything comprehensible or reasonable I could raise would immediately be refuted by the "Well, we don't know how it could have evolved yet" argument.
That's riiiiight. That's how this kind of discussion works. There's a trump-card of an argument against IC. Irreducible complexity essentially follows the form "I cannot conceive of how this evolved, therefore it did not." This is such a simply incorrect form of reasoning that it can be dismissed without much effort. Personal incredulity (which is the basis of IC) is not evidence of impossibility.

#21224 1 2008-08-24T08:40:01Z DemonzLunchBreak
Here are my poorly-formed caffeine-inspired thoughts from 1 AM. You're Welcome.

It seems to me that the vast majority of philosophical disputes that I come across these days can be accounted for simply by linguistic confusion. Most "confusing" philosophical dilemmas only seem so because the language involved is confused, which results in poor thinking. The whole Idealism/Materialism debate is a good example of this. In this context, "perceptions" and "objects" are really just different-sounding labels for exactly the same phenomena. The meaning of the words is independent of the pressure vibrations in the air or the shapes of the written symbols that carry those meanings. What the Idealist refers to as "forms" or "thoughts" are perceptions of the same phenomena that a materialist calls "matter." Meaning is what ends up being significant, and not the terminology involved.

Pragmatism has a similar kind of issue. The pragmatic theory of truth is that that which is useful to believe is true. People think that this is somehow a separate idea from say, correspondence theory of truth (that which corresponds to reality is true), but that's clearly not true; it's just an unnecessary (and confusing) redefining of the word "truth." When people talk about something being true, typically, they mean what correspondence theory says. It's a semantic trick on the part of the pragmatists to call useful propositions true. Useful propositions are useful. Pragmatists are really people who advocate usefulness over truth. However, they do this in the most confusing way possible, by redefining a word that already has a commonly understood definition.

"Free Will" is another example of a linguistically confused concept. I can hardly find two people who agree on what those two words even mean. Most determinists agree completely on what exists, but are confused in their terminology. Most people, whether aware of it or not, believe in an essentially deterministic universe. Tsukatu/Strife and I talked about this a while back, we agreed, pretty much, about what existed in the universe, we were just arguing about what to call all of these things. That alone wouldn't be a big issue, except that for a while I thought there was some genuine disagreement - and that is why linguistic confusion is a real issue.

I'm just as guilty of this as the next guy. I dunno if Dave remembers, but we had a discussion-type-thing a while back. My entire argument was nothing more than some semantic contortionism. He saw that as bullshit, and pounced on that right away. That was an important lesson for me. I learned that confusing people with Latin and equivocation was no way to conduct a discussion.

Now, obviously, there are real disagreements in philosophy, but I'm starting to think that they're few and far between.

When I think, I've found that I don't usually think in words, but rather in abstractions and meanings. This is cool for when my thinking is stuck in my own head, but when I'm trying to communicate to others, it's not exactly helpful. I try to write, but it never comes out the way I want it to. I'm normally pretty happy. Or even-keeled at the least, but lately I've been feeling this sort of existential anguish without really understanding why. I feel like I know the answer to all of these questions I have, but there's something going wrong in the process that converts these abstractions into words, and that's adding to the frustration.

It feels like when I post in the SD, I'm only criticizing the ideas of others, and not really putting my own forward. I don't mean to do this, but it ends up happening because any time I try to put a thesis forward, it ends up being unrefined and sounding wrong when I read it over. This makes me think about whether it was ever even correct in the first place. It's not that I'm afraid of being wrong, it's more that I don't want to contribute something that I think is wrong or shaky.

I have more things that I'm thinking about, but they'll have to come later because I'm falling asleep right now. This topic is my thought toilet. Feel free to do the same - dump whatever's on your mind. I feel like if I can write down whatever I'm brooding over, it becomes less of an issue and my brain can relax a little more. If any moderator thinks this is a bad idea or this is in the wrong place, let me know and I'll shut up.

In conclusion, Bone Thugs-n-Harmony is amazing.

Quote: blue_tetris, 2008-08-24T23:33:48Z
I feel bad for computational linguists. Plenty of things are objective, but language is necessarily subjective. We create it, expand it, and innovate on its terms every day. If a majority doesn't agree with a definition for a word, then in what way does that definition describe the word's usage?
Haha, good trolling. Where is Strife, anyway? I want to know what he thinks about this stuff.

Words aren't owned by the majority, they're the "property" of the parties that use them. Unless you're dealing with one set of canonical definitions (e.g. those found in English dictionaries), a word could conceivably mean anything. A word is just an inert symbol. The meaning of a given word is situational - it depends on what linguistic framework is being used. If you're speaking English, words have true and objective definitions. They're the ones that you find in dictionaries. If you're speaking from some kind of specialized framework (the way most people talk) that isn't quite English as it's found in dictionaries, then words can mean whatever the people talking want.

If you want to talk about Tsukatu's definition of atheism... well... his definition isn't objectively true (as if those were adjectives that even make sense to apply to a definition for a word). But his definition makes sense to use in the context of philosophical discussion, which is a place full of highly-specialized linguistic frameworks.

And here I am, making up terminology. Fuck. Whenever I try to think about this kind of thing, it always ends with metacognition.
